sentences.text: The known fossil material consists of parts of a right wing, including the humerus, ulna, and radius.
Comparisons with ground bird wing bones suggest Piksi was about the size of a common pheasant, with a wingspan estimated to have been perhaps 80 cm or slightly less.
The animal may have weighed between 500 grams and 1 kilogram.
The species name barbarulna means "strange elbowed big bird", combining Blackfoot words for "big bird" or "chicken" with the Latin word for "strange" and the bone name "ulna".
Gloria Jean Siebrecht discovered the fossils in 1991 on the Blackfeet Indian Reservation.
David J. Varricchio described the genus in 2002.
The only known specimens are housed in the Museum of the Rockies under collection number MOR 1113.
The bones were found in a silty claystone deposit.
The fossil site was inland, at least 350 km from the coast of the Western Interior Seaway.
The sediment likely formed from a small floodplain or ephemeral pool.
Agnolin and Varricchio (2012) reinterpreted Piksi as a pterosaur instead of a bird.
Recent studies suggest affinities for the suborder Pteranodontoidea.
The species is classified within the suborder Pterodactyloidea.
The species belongs to the superfamily Ornithocheiroidea.
The time range for Piksi is the Campanian stage, from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.
It is debated whether Piksi is a pterosaur, as its humerus possesses features found in theropods but not in any pterodactyloid pterosaurs.
